newsitem.title: USA: Democrats threaten to pull out of funds probe.
newsitem.headline: Democrats threaten to pull out of funds probe.

text.p: Democrats on the Senate committee looking into campaign fund-raising scandals threatened Thursday to pull out of the investigation, saying Republicans had turned it into a witch-hunt against Democrats.
Ohio Sen. John Glenn, the ranking Democrat on the Senate governmental affairs committee, said the Republican majority was hiding the misdeeds of their party and focusing exclusively on Democrats.

Glenn, flanked by four other Democrats from the committee, told a news conference: "If we get to the point where we feel .. it's just a sham, a charade of what it was supposed to be, are we going to participate in that?
"No, there will come a point where we will say, they are going to have to make it a Democratic witch-hunt which is what they're trying to make it anyway, and do it on their own."
"Is it worth going on? This is something we have to determine," Glenn added.

The other Democrats supported Glenn. Michigan Sen. Carl Levin said: "We are not going to participate in a partisan charade." New Jersey Sen. Robert Torricelli said: "This is very close to breaking down. It has lost all credibility."

The committee was investigating whether China and other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by helping President Bill Clinton and the Democratic Party with illegal political contributions.
The Democratic Party has promised to return some $3 million which were apparently illegally raised from foreign interests, mainly Asian corporations and businessmen.

Democrats would also like to probe possible Republican financial links to foreign business interests. The Republicans have returned some $122,000 raised for a party think tank from a Hong Kong company.
The FBI and a House committee were conducting simultaneous but separate investigations.

Committee chairman, Sen. Fred Thompson of Tennessee, hoped to begin public hearings in July, but the Democratic news conference indicated that chances of conducting a bipartisan investigation were pratically dead.
Glenn's main complaints was that the Republicans had refused most of his requests to issue subpoenas to groups associated with the Republicans.
Where such subpoenas have been issued, they have either been ignored or, in the case of the Republican National Committee, the documents were heavily edited with large parts blacked out, he said.
Paul Clark, communications director for the committee who speaks for the Republican majority, said Glenn was trying to protect Democrats who were stonewalling the investigation.
For instance, the Democratic Party had sent the committee thousands of pages of documents but most were useless or irrelevant, Clark said.
Most key players in the scandal have either gone to Asia or indicated their intention of invoking their Fifth Amendment rights not to testify.

The latest to do so were 16 Buddhist monks who received subpoenas from the committee last month. Their temple hosted a fund-raising event last year addressed by Vice President Al Gore, in possible violation of its tax exempt status as a religious institution.
